note: An AD-HOC reference CONSTRUCTED between just these two agents for just this exchange — not adopted from any standard. Minimal: one entry per shared seam category the exchange needs, each fixed by a canonical example both sides can instantiate. It deliberately does NOT cover either side's native concepts (grade, bearer, vlan, service), which is how it pre-empts the cross-domain 'grade' false cognate. Each definition pins a requirement so it cannot be silently misread across domains.

entries.label: transport underlay
entries.definition: The transport circuit that carries an IP service as its underlay — the one object both domains share, owned by transport and consumed by IP.
entries.example: Meridian circuit CIR-7 is the underlay of Cascade service SVC-42

entries.label: demarcation point
entries.definition: The single point where the transport circuit hands off to, and the IP service attaches at, the customer site — one demarcation seen from both sides.
entries.example: the NY demarcation: Meridian hand-off ho-NY-CIR7 is the same point as Cascade attachment att-NY-SVC42

entries.label: committed service rate
entries.definition: The committed client payload rate the service guarantees — NOT the bearer line rate. Pinned to committed payload to prevent the line-rate / committed-rate confusion.
entries.example: 5 Gbit/s committed (not the 100 Gbit/s bearer line rate)

entries.label: latency bound
entries.definition: The one-way latency the service must not exceed, however each side expresses it — a number of milliseconds on the transport side, a named tier on the IP side. Pinned to a bound, not a measured metric.
entries.example: <= 8 ms one-way is the same requirement as latency tier T2

entries.label: path protection
entries.definition: Protection of the service against a failure of the transport PATH (a fiber cut or bearer loss) — pinned to a path/underlay failure, distinct from an IP scheduling class.
entries.example: survive a single fiber cut on CIR-7's primary path by switching to the diverse path
